sentences.text: Let's go back to that evening.
The emperor, as we saw, had gone to Hagia Sophia.
He had never been crowned in that church.
Tonight, he may have been saying goodbye to it.
Then came the order that sealed the defenders in.
As Giustiniani and his Greek and Italian comrades passed through the inner wall to take their places at the outer wall and the stockade, the gates of the inner wall were shut behind them.
There was to be no retreat.
Remember that detail too.
The assault began between one and two hours after midnight.
First came the irregulars, the bashi-bazouks, wave after wave, meant to tire the defenders and cheap to lose.
Then the troops from Anatolia.
Both were thrown back.
For about an hour, even the Janissaries, the sultan's own household infantry, could make no headway.
Which brings us to the suspects.
Let's take them one at a time.
Suspect number one: the cannon.
The case against it is simple.
For six weeks, the guns had hammered the same stretch of wall.
They breached it in three places, and on the Sunday before the final night, three direct hits from the great gun brought down part of the stockade.
The case for the defense is just as simple.
Every night, the stockade went back up, and when the assault came, it was still there.
The cannon opened the door.
It did not walk through it.
Suspect number two: a small door.
The Kerkoporta was a little sally port, half hidden by a tower, where an old wall met the great Theodosian wall.
The story you'll find in many books is that somebody left it open, and Turkish soldiers wandered in.
That comes mainly from one chronicler, Ducas.
Critobulus, who wrote for the sultan, doesn't mention it at all.
Excavations haven't found a matching gate.
Which makes you wonder.
But the Italian brothers called Bocchiardi were using the little door that very night, to strike back at the Turkish troops.
Runciman, writing in nineteen sixty-five, doesn't blame a careless guard.
In his telling, the door was open because defenders were using it.
Suspect number three: Giustiniani.
Just before sunrise, a shot fired at close range struck him and pierced his breastplate.
Runciman says his nerve broke, and he demanded to be taken away.
The emperor himself begged him to stay.
A gate was opened, and his bodyguard carried him through the streets to a Genoese ship in the harbor.
Before the gate could be shut again, the Genoese around him came streaming through after him.
Barbaro, the Venetian, claimed the wound was nothing and that Giustiniani faked it out of fear.
But the wound was real.
He died of it on Chios a day or two later.
Whether his nerve failed is another question, and his own people answered it much more kindly than the Venetians did.
And then, suddenly, someone looked up and saw Turkish flags flying from the tower above the Kerkoporta.
The cry went up: the city is taken.
Do you see it?
These aren't three suspects.
They're three links.
The cannon cracked the stockade.
The bullet found Giustiniani.
The fear, and the open gate, did the rest.
Take away any one of them and the night might have gone differently.
Or it might not.
Runciman himself says that even if Giustiniani hadn't been wounded and the little door hadn't been left ajar, little would have changed in the long run.
The emperor was told that the Turks were inside.
According to Critobulus, he cried out that the city was taken and he was still alive.

Then he dismounted, and with three companions, his cousin Theophilus Palaiologos, a Spaniard called Don Francisco of Toledo, and a soldier named John Dalmata, he held the approach to the gate for a few minutes.
They tried to rally the Greeks.
The Greeks were beyond rallying.
The gate was jammed with men trying to get out, and more and more Janissaries were falling on them.
Theophilus shouted that he would rather die than live, and disappeared into the oncoming hordes.
And that's the last we see of Constantine Palaiologos.
Nobody who wrote about it actually saw how he died.
Critobulus says he fell fighting.
Leonard says a Janissary struck him down.
Ducas says his head was recognized and displayed.
Phrantzes says a body wearing imperial eagles was found and given to Christians to bury.
Barbaro says some claimed to have seen him among the dead, and others that he was never found.
Pears judged that none of these accounts is quite trustworthy, and no one knows where he lies.
Later, a legend grew that an angel turned him to marble and hid him under the Golden Gate, to wait.
That one has very little support in the early sources.
Which has not stopped anyone from telling it.
By about five or six in the morning, the city was in Turkish hands.
The killing went on for hours, until about midday, by the account of Critobulus.
Then the soldiers worked out that prisoners and treasure were worth more than corpses.
Critobulus counts about four thousand dead.
More than fifty thousand people, by his count, were taken as slaves.
Leonard of Chios says sixty thousand.
Whichever number you trust, it was the end of a world for the people in it.
The sultan had come at dawn to look at the breach, with the waning moon still high in the sky.
Then he waited until afternoon, when the first excesses of massacre and pillage were over, to make his own entry.
He rode to Hagia Sophia.
A soldier was prying up a piece of the marble floor.
Mehmed struck him.
The loot and the captives, he said, were the army's.
The buildings were his.
An imam climbed into the pulpit, and the Great Church became a mosque.
And then came the irony that Gennadius, the monk who had warned that the city would fall, was named patriarch by the sultan himself.
"Be patriarch, and be at peace," Mehmed is reported to have said.
The sultan took the title Caesar of Rome, on the grounds that whoever held Constantinople held the Roman Empire.
He moved his capital there.
Many historians use that year as the end of the Middle Ages, though like most such dates, it's a convenience.
What's less of a convenience is that the age of the great wall was over.
A big enough gun, and the money to build it, could do what a thousand years of armies could not.
There were stranger endings still.
Constantine's own nephews were taken into the sultan's household.
One of them, renamed Mesih Pasha, rose to be admiral of the Ottoman fleet and went on to serve twice as grand vizier.
Cardinal Isidore, the Pope's man, who had come to proclaim the union in Hagia Sophia, was captured too.
He was reportedly ransomed for a few small coins.
The empire's last defenders died, fled, or changed sides.
And the city itself became, within a generation, one of the great capitals of a new empire.
Runciman lists the ifs, and he lists them kindly.
A less determined sultan.
A more persuasive vizier.
A Venetian fleet that sailed a fortnight earlier.
Change any one, and Byzantium might have lingered on for another decade.
Not much longer.
So which suspect do I arrest?
None of them.
Or all three, which in a courtroom comes to the same thing.
A twenty-one-year-old with a gun he'd bought from the other side.
A wall that had held for a thousand years, held by fewer than seven thousand people.
A wounded man, a door, and a few minutes of fear.
That's the part I keep coming back to.
The walls didn't fall because they were weak.
They fell because, for one hour, at dawn, on one patch of ground, the people holding them ran out of the only thing a wall can't supply: more people.
Go back to the evening of the twenty-eighth.
The emperor rides to the Great Church.
He prays.
By dawn, it will all be over.
And somewhere, the legend says, the last Roman emperor sleeps on, in marble, under a gate in a wall that no longer stands guard.
The truth is quieter.
Nobody knows where Constantine lies.
All we know is that on the morning of the twenty-ninth of May, the waning moon was still high in the sky when the sultan came to look at the breach.
If you'd like more stories told this way, you know where to find us.
Thank you for listening.
